analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set safe nurse staffing plans and post staffing levels publicly.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to require safe nurse staffing at Medicare hospitals died in committee with 22 cosponsors and never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to write a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan, developed by a committee where direct-care nurses hold the majority, with adjustable minimums for registered nurses on every unit and shift. Hospitals would have to post daily staffing levels where patients can see them, report staffing and quality data to Medicare, and let nurses refuse assignments that violate the plan or that they are not trained for. It also barred hospitals from retaliating against patients or employees who complain, with fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. The bill never got a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would get care under staffing levels tied in the bill's findings to fewer falls, infections, medication errors, and deaths, plus public staffing information to compare hospitals. Registered nurses also gain: a majority seat on the committees that set staffing, the right to refuse unsafe assignments, overtime policies set by the committee, and whistleblower protection with court remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare-participating hospital would have to implement a staffing plan requiring an appropriate number of registered nurses on each unit and each shift, aimed at safe, quality care, with the plan written by a committee where at least 55% of members are direct-care registered nurses rather than managers or administrators.

Hospitals would have to post daily, in a visible place, how many licensed and unlicensed nursing staff are caring for patients in each unit, and publish staffing plans and committee evaluations, with the data also posted on Medicare's Hospital Compare website in plain language so patients can compare hospitals.

Nurses could refuse an assignment that violates the hospital's staffing plan or that they are not educated, trained, or experienced to handle safely, and hospitals could not discriminate or retaliate against patients or employees for complaining — with prevailing employees entitled to reinstatement, lost wages, and attorney's fees, and prevailing patients entitled to $5,000 in liquidated damages.

The bill cites research in its findings that higher registered nurse staffing is linked to lower rates of falls, infections, medication errors, and death, and that inadequate staffing contributed to 24% of unanticipated events causing patient death, injury, or permanent loss of function.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare-participating hospitals, which would bear the cost of meeting staffing minimums, running committees, posting and reporting data, and potential civil money penalties — all as a condition of their Medicare provider agreement, with no new federal funding attached. Those costs could be passed on to patients and insurers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals would absorb the cost of higher nurse staffing and new reporting duties with no dedicated federal funding, as a condition of Medicare participation; those costs could be passed to patients and insurers through higher hospital prices.

The bill sets no fixed nurse-to-patient ratio: minimums would be 'adjustable' numbers set by each hospital's own committee, and the plan could include exemptions during declared emergencies — so a hospital-friendly committee could write a weak plan and understaffing could persist in practice.

Enforcement is soft: civil money penalties are capped at $10,000 per knowing violation (higher only for a pattern of violations), and a provision wipes a hospital's published penalties from the federal website one year after a change of ownership — a carve-out that benefits buyers of penalized hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety case is strong — the bill's own findings tie staffing levels to deaths, infections, and errors, and it gives nurses real leverage (committee majorities, refusal rights, whistleblower protection) plus public transparency. But the design is a compromise: no fixed ratios, committee-set minimums, emergency exemptions, and modest fines mean a determined hospital could comply on paper while keeping staffing thin. Hospitals bear real costs without new funding, some of which would likely reach patients and insurers as higher prices. A stronger bill would have set firmer floors and penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the bill on June 15, 2010, joined as original cosponsors by Republicans Steve LaTourette and Ginny Brown-Waite.

The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee; the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
It finished with 22 cosponsors — 16 of 253 House Democrats and 6 of 178 House Republicans — and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals came out ahead: they avoided federal staffing requirements, public daily staffing disclosure, and fines. Hospital patients and nurses gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 16 of 253 House Democrats and 6 of 178 House Republicans — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no voting record to show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Every Medicare-participating hospital would face binding staffing plans set by nurse-majority committees, daily public posting of staffing levels, quality-data reporting, fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation, and whistleblower liability — with no new funding. What costs hospitals here is precisely what would give patients safer care and nurses safer conditions.

Direct-care nurses would hold at least 55% of the staffing committee, gain the right to refuse unsafe assignments, get committee-set overtime and relief policies, and receive whistleblower protection with court remedies. Better staffing also addresses the burnout and turnover the bill's findings describe.
